opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most important open questions right now, because the way we build these models today assumes the world is static. We pretrain on a giant snapshot of data, and then the model is essentially frozen in time. But the world keeps changing: new events, new facts, new terminology, even new ways people use language.

The naive answer is to keep fine-tuning on new data, but that turns out to be surprisingly tricky. When you fine-tune on a small amount of new information, models often don't really absorb it in a way they can use flexibly. They might memorize a sentence but fail to answer a question that requires reasoning about it. And at the same time, you can damage what the model already knew, the classic forgetting problem. There's also the issue that fine-tuning on unfamiliar facts can encourage hallucination, because you're teaching the model to confidently produce things it doesn't have a grounded understanding of.

Retrieval is the other big approach: keep the model fixed and give it access to fresh documents at inference time. That works well in many cases, but it puts a lot of burden on the model to reconcile what's in its context with what's in its weights, and models aren't always good at deciding which to trust when they conflict.

So my view is that we need to design for updatability from the start rather than treating it as an afterthought. That means thinking about pretraining and fine-tuning objectives that make knowledge easier to edit and extend later, understanding which parts of a model actually store knowledge versus skills, and developing better ways to combine parametric knowledge with retrieval so the model knows when it's uncertain or out of date. Ideally, a model should be a bit like a person who keeps learning: able to integrate new information without overwriting everything it learned before, and aware of the limits of what it knows.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fine-tuning and retrieval as ways to keep models current, but does not argue that repeatedly training models from scratch will become infeasible.

r002.rationale: It says models struggle to reconcile fresh documents in context with knowledge in their weights and may not know which to trust when they conflict.

r003.rationale: The response mentions separating stored knowledge from skills and learning without overwriting prior knowledge, but does not pose how to disentangle what to preserve from what to update.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because I think the way we currently approach it is kind of fundamentally mismatched with what we actually want. Right now the dominant paradigm is: you pretrain on a giant static snapshot of the internet, and then if the world changes, you either retrieve from some external source at inference time, or you just... retrain from scratch, or you do some fine-tuning and hope you don't break anything.

And I think each of those has real problems. Retrieval is great for a certain class of facts, like, who won the election, what's the current price of something. But a lot of what it means to be "up to date" isn't a lookup. It's more like, the way people talk about a topic has shifted, a new library has become the standard way to do something, the consensus in a field has moved. That's not a fact you can retrieve, that's something that needs to be absorbed into how the model reasons. And retrieval doesn't really get you that.

So then the question becomes, can we just keep training these models continually? And the honest answer is that we're pretty bad at it. You run into catastrophic forgetting, where you learn the new thing and quietly lose old capabilities. And there's a subtler issue, which is that learning from new data at scale is surprisingly fragile. Models seem to lose plasticity as they're trained further. The more you've trained, the harder it gets to take on genuinely new information efficiently. And a lot of our understanding of that is still pretty shallow.

So if I were to say how I think they should be designed, I'd say a few things. One, we should probably treat updatability as a first-class design goal rather than something we bolt on afterward. That might mean architectural choices, like having some parts of the model that are explicitly meant to be the "fast-changing" knowledge versus the stable reasoning core. Two, I think we need much better evaluation of what it even means to be up to date, because right now we mostly test with trivia-style questions, and that misses the harder, more diffuse kinds of staleness. And three, there's a science question underneath all of this about why continual learning is hard for these models, and I think we need to actually understand that, rather than just throwing more tricks at it.

So I don't think I have a clean answer, but I do think the framing of "pretrain once, patch forever" is the wrong one, and we should be designing for models that are expected to keep learning.

r001.rationale: It mentions retraining from scratch as one current approach, but does not argue that repeated scratch training will eventually become infeasible.

r002.rationale: It says retrieval does not let diffuse changes become part of the model’s reasoning, but does not state that models struggle to override parametric knowledge with information supplied in context.

r003.rationale: It proposes separating fast-changing knowledge from a stable reasoning core, conveying the design question of what to update versus preserve.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate what a model needs to learn from what it needs to look up. You want the model to learn how to reason with information, but you probably don’t want updating a fact to require retraining the entire model. So retrieval is a natural component: let the model access information that can be updated independently of its parameters.

But access alone isn’t enough. What happens when the retrieved information conflicts with something the model learned during training? Can it recognize which source is more current, use that information appropriately, and acknowledge when the evidence is insufficient? Those are capabilities we need to design for and evaluate.

So I’d think of staying up to date as a property of the whole system—the model, its sources, and how it decides what to trust—rather than just how recently we trained it.

r001.rationale: The response says updating a fact should not require retraining the entire model, but does not argue that repeatedly training new models from scratch will eventually become infeasible.

r002.rationale: It raises conflicts between retrieved information and learned knowledge, but does not clearly state that language models can struggle to override their parametric knowledge with in-context information.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes what the model should learn from what it should look up and update independently, conveying the preserve-versus-update design question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should separate what a model needs to learn during training from what it can look up when it answers a question. Training should give it the ability to reason and use information, but it’s probably not the right way to keep every fact up to date. You don’t want to retrain a model every time something changes.

So I’d like models to be able to consult an evolving source of information, recognize when their own knowledge might be stale, and decide when to retrieve something new. But retrieval alone doesn’t solve the problem. The model still has to assess whether a source is reliable, handle conflicting information, and be willing to say, “I don’t have enough evidence.” Staying up to date is partly about access to fresh information, and partly about knowing how to use it.

r001.rationale: It says retraining for every change is undesirable, but does not argue that repeatedly training models from scratch will eventually become infeasible.

r002.rationale: It discusses retrieval and stale knowledge, but does not say models struggle to override parametric knowledge with information in context.

r003.rationale: It separates what models should learn during training from facts they can look up and update when answering.
